# Human Interface 04 | Design systems, responsive interfaces and accessibility

[← Case studies](03_UX_CASE_STUDIES.md) · [Volume VI](../OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Next: Measuring usability →](05_MEASURE_USABILITY.md)

A design system is not a gallery of pretty buttons. It is a shared set of decisions that helps people build predictable interfaces without re-solving every interaction.

My cross-stack experience makes this important: I have worked with reporting interfaces, React applications, native-mobile ambitions and administrative tools. Every inconsistent control adds a small cognitive cost, and those costs accumulate.

## Start with principles

- **Meaning:** text, icons and colour should communicate the same state.
- **Consistency:** one action should look and behave similarly across related screens.
- **Feedback:** loading, success, partial success, warning and failure should be distinct.
- **Access:** keyboard, touch, zoom, assistive technology and different devices matter.
- **Restraint:** visual effects should support hierarchy rather than distract from work.
- **Truth:** never style a draft state so it resembles a completed transaction.

## Tokens that carry meaning

~~~css
:root {
  --surface: #101f2b;
  --surface-raised: #1a3443;
  --text-primary: #f3f7f8;
  --text-muted: #c6d6dc;
  --accent: #75e8d4;
  --warning: #f1ce84;
  --danger: #ffb6aa;
  --focus-ring: 3px solid var(--warning);
  --radius-control: 0.65rem;
}
~~~

These are **illustrative OmniMaster design tokens**, not a claim that all my production applications share a formal component library. A real system would validate contrast for every foreground/background combination and interaction state.

## Design a component around behaviour

Consider a **Submit & Sync** button.

| State | Visible behaviour | Underlying requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Ready | Clear label and action | User authorised, input valid |
| Processing | “Syncing…” with progress or status | Prevent unintended duplicate submissions |
| Partial result | “37 imported, 3 need review” | Backend supports partial-result semantics |
| Complete | Confirmation plus useful next step | Transaction actually committed |
| Failed safely | Explanation and retry/recovery path | Server knows what changed and what did not |
| Not permitted | Disabled/hidden only for clarity | Server must independently deny the request |

A single spinner cannot represent the whole workflow.

## Accessibility is a development responsibility

Use semantic HTML and labels first; add ARIA when native semantics do not supply the needed information. Respect visible focus, correct tab order, zoom and reflow, reduced-motion preferences, meaningful alt text and feedback to assistive technology.

For data charts, provide understandable titles, units and a text/table alternative. Don't rely only on red/green to distinguish performance. For forms, show exactly which field needs correction and preserve previously entered valid information where safe.

**Standard to study:** WCAG 2.2 AA is a useful design and test target. A small unit-test suite or Lighthouse result does not certify complete compliance.

## Responsive, not merely smaller

~~~css
.dashboard {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after { scroll-behavior: auto; animation-duration: 0.01ms; }
}
~~~

A layout that technically fits at 320 pixels may still be difficult to use. Check tap targets, column priority, sticky headers, long identifiers, error messages and the real task flow on representative devices.

## The test pyramid for interfaces

| Test | Helps detect | Does not guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Component/unit | Wrong local state or error copy | User comprehends the flow |
| Responsive visual | Overflow, clipping, theme regression | Touch/keyboard accessibility |
| Accessibility automation | Many semantic, contrast and label issues | Every WCAG requirement |
| Keyboard/manual | Focus order, traps, usable controls | Every screen-reader interaction |
| Assistive technology | Announcements and interaction behaviour | Population-wide task success |
| Moderated usability study | Confusion, hesitation, wrong turns | Universal needs from a tiny sample |
| Operational telemetry | Error rates and workflow drop-off | The reason for a failure without further research |

## A mini design system exercise

Implement one **upload status card** with four statuses: idle, uploading, validated and failed. Define its tokens and component props. Use a status heading and text, not colour alone. Include a keyboard-visible Retry action.

Ask a colleague to explain each state without hearing your interpretation. If they cannot, revise the wording and hierarchy before adding animation.

## What I'd like to sharpen

I want to improve consistency across web and native experiences, documented design decisions, accessibility in interactive data visualisation, and validation with real users. The outcome I care about is a dependable experience, not an arbitrary design-tool score.

# Human Interface 05 | Testing whether an experience works

[← Design systems](04_DESIGN_SYSTEMS_AND_ACCESSIBILITY.md) · [Volume VI](../OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Next: UX workbook →](06_UX_WORKBOOK.md)

**A successful build is not evidence that a person completed their task.** My experience engineering reporting and applications taught me to care about functional correctness. UX requires an additional question: can a person find, understand and accomplish the goal in their context?

## Define a testable task

Bad test: “What do you think of this dashboard?”

Better task: “Find the three deliveries needing attention today, and explain which one you would investigate first.”

The second reveals navigation, information hierarchy, comprehension and decision-making. It doesn't ask the participant to validate your taste.

## Five practical measurements

| Measurement | What it tells us | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Task completion** | Did the person reach the defined result? | A completion can still be slow or stressful |
| **Time on task** | How much effort does the journey require? | Faster is not always better for consequential decisions |
| **Error rate** | How often are mistakes or invalid submissions made? | System constraints can create artificial errors |
| **Recovery success** | Can the person correct an error without help? | Requires a meaningful error scenario |
| **Understanding / confidence** | Can they interpret the result and next action? | Self-reported confidence isn't proof of correctness |

For data-heavy interfaces, include **time to correct insight**: how long until the user identifies the actual business exception, not merely a visible number.

## How I'd run a small study

1. **Choose a representative task** and one realistic scenario.
2. **Recruit an appropriate participant** with consent; explain purpose and privacy.
3. **Avoid leading language.** Ask what the person expects the control to do.
4. **Observe actions and hesitation** without teaching during the task.
5. **Record outcome**, errors, confusing labels, and recovery attempts.
6. **Change one high-impact issue** and test the revision.
7. **Report limitations:** small samples produce leads, not statistical certainty.

You can start with a colleague and fictional data, but don't claim broad user validation from one session.

## Ethical research boundaries

Do not record sensitive financial, school or employee records simply because a test involves such a product. Use approved fictional accounts and get permission before collecting video, audio, feedback or identifiers. Store only what the study needs, restrict access and set a retention plan.

If a participant needs assistive technology, let them use their normal setup; don't treat accessibility as a trick question.

## Example usability study: the Study Room link

**Observed feedback:** a reader clicks “Interactive Study Room” and lands in GitHub's HTML source viewer instead of a usable learning interface.

**Task:** open the study room and answer the first question.

**Original outcome:** task blocked at navigation.

**Intervention:** host the HTML as an actual web experience, replace the prominent link, and retain a separate link for source inspection.

**Acceptance check:** the live URL returns a rendered HTML page and the first scenario can be selected and explained using keyboard or pointer. Check the deployment and real browser behaviour separately; a CI source check alone is not enough.

A small bug, but a useful teaching example of why **link destination, naming and expectation are UX work**.

## A study report template

~~~text
Study objective:
User group / context:
Task:
What success looks like:
Device / accessibility context:
Consent and data policy:
Observed completion:
Wrong turns and errors:
Where the participant hesitated:
Direct quotes (with permission):
Interpretation versus actual observation:
Proposed change:
Verification after change:
Remaining uncertainty:
~~~

## Don't optimise the wrong thing

A page loading in 400 milliseconds is irrelevant if people cannot find the action. A high click-through rate can be misleading if users click repeatedly because feedback is absent. A beautiful graph is not a correct business explanation.

Metrics should connect to **human outcomes** and system correctness, not simply demonstrate activity.

## Learning exercise

Take the [OmniMaster Arcade](../OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md) or [online Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/). Ask a friend to begin a scenario with no instructions. Observe whether they understand the choices, find feedback, navigate to the next case and interpret their progress.

Write three improvements ranked by impact and effort. Implement one, then test again.

# Human Interface 06 | Practical UI/UX workbook

[← Measuring usability](05_MEASURE_USABILITY.md) · [Volume VI](../OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Academy](../OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md)

This workbook teaches you to improve an interface through observation, not by guessing which design trend is fashionable.

All scenarios use fictional data. You can work in plain HTML, React or a design tool, but at least one exercise must become a usable browser interaction.

## Mission A. Rewrite a confusing flow

**Scenario:** a fictional integration platform has four identical-looking buttons: Test, Preview, Stage and Sync.

**Goal:** distinguish operations with labels, descriptions and appropriate confirmation.

**Deliverable:** a before/after flow diagram and prototype.

**Pass criterion:** a new user can correctly explain which actions read data and which persist changes before clicking.

<details>
<summary>My reasoning</summary>

I would show tasks in the order users need them, explain consequences and make the confirmed durable-write step distinct. “Preview” should be clearly read-only. The response must reflect actual backend semantics.

</details>

## Mission B. Fix an error message

**Scenario:** “Error 500: upload failed.”

**Goal:** help a user recover without falsely claiming that nothing changed.

**Deliverable:** error-state component with message, reference ID and safe next step.

**Pass criterion:** the person knows whether to retry, inspect a status or contact support. Verify every factual promise against backend behaviour.

## Mission C. Redesign a dashboard for a phone

**Scenario:** a desktop dashboard contains twelve cards, a wide chart and four global filters.

**Goal:** prioritise the one operational decision the person needs on a narrow screen.

**Deliverable:** mobile wireframe, prioritisation rationale, reflow and keyboard/touch check.

**Pass criterion:** the primary task can be completed without zooming to find an unlabeled control.

## Mission D. Make a chart accessible

**Scenario:** status is shown using red, amber and green lines with no textual explanation.

**Goal:** communicate series, units, changes and actions without colour-only meaning.

**Deliverable:** accessible chart label, legend, text equivalent and summary table.

**Pass criterion:** a user can determine the important status using text alone.

## Mission E. Build a form people can repair

**Scenario:** a school assessment form clears all answers after one invalid field.

**Goal:** preserve valid work, identify the problem and communicate what was and was not saved.

**Deliverable:** form states, validation strategy and failure simulation.

**Pass criterion:** a user corrects the field and completes the task without unnecessary re-entry.

## Mission F. Design a human AI review

**Scenario:** an AI system suggests a learner grade with a quote from an approved passage.

**Goal:** ensure the educator can examine, reject or correct the suggestion.

**Deliverable:** review screen with source evidence, rubric boundaries, audit note and explicit approve/reject state.

**Pass criterion:** the grade is not silently accepted because the model sounded confident.

## Mission G. Repair a broken link journey

**Scenario:** a prominently labelled “Launch interactive experience” link opens a source-code viewer.

**Goal:** fix the information architecture and destination.

**Deliverable:** live-page link, separate source link and a user-journey test.

**Pass criterion:** the visitor reaches the interactive page and completes its first action; not merely a 200 response for a repository README.

## Mission H. Run a usability mini-study

Recruit a willing participant using fictional content. Give them one task without coaching. Record completion, errors, confusion and recovery. Document the problem, propose an intervention, retest and disclose the sample size.

**Deliverable:** one-page research note with observation and follow-up test.

**Pass criterion:** the change follows evidence rather than personal preference.

---

## A simple UX review rubric

| Area | Weak | Better | Strong |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Discoverability** | User guesses where to go | Navigation is labelled | The intended task is obvious and findable |
| **Clarity** | Jargon or unlabeled metrics | Helpful labels | Purpose, scope, period and consequences are clear |
| **Feedback** | Silent request | Success/error message | Accurate status, next step and recovery |
| **Accessibility** | Mouse/colour only | Basic semantic controls | Keyboard, contrast, focus, zoom and assistive-tech checks |
| **Responsive design** | Overflow | Screen fits | Priority and workflow adapt to device |
| **Trust** | Stale or AI output looks definitive | Some caveats | Provenance, uncertainty and decision ownership explicit |
| **Evidence** | “Looks good” | Peer opinion | Observed task outcomes and tested revisions |

Score yourself by identifying the weakest criterion and fixing it. A subjective sum across categories is not a certification.

## The personal challenge

Take one interface from your public portfolio. Explain **who it serves, what success means, which details matter to the user, and what you changed after observing friction**.

That is the kind of UI/UX case study I want to build more of: actual reasoning and measured improvement rather than a screenshot gallery.

[← Volume VI](../OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [My UX story](01_MY_UX_JOURNEY.md) · [Interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/)

# Build With Me 01 | Define the source before building a pipeline

[← Volume V](../OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Next: Ingestion →](02_INGESTION_AND_TRANSACTIONS.md)

## The first question I ask

**What happened in the real world, and what does one record mean?**

In enterprise BI and manufacturing, I learned that a source system often stores what was convenient for its users, not what an analytics engineer expects. A delivery, invoice, account update, school progression decision and audit event have different identities and timing semantics.

This chapter uses **fictional account updates** only. It is not a bank ledger.

## Step 1. Read the event contract

Open [engine.py](../../projects/data-to-decision-platform/engine.py) and find the `Event` dataclass. It contains:

| Field | Why it exists | What the demo assumes |
|---|---|---|
| `event_id` | Identifies one submitted source change | Unique and stable across retry |
| `position` | Identifies where a change sits in a fictional source stream | One unique positive integer per event |
| `tenant` and `account` | Identify the business entity | One current state per tenant/account |
| `version` | Distinguishes newer from older account states | Strict integer that increases per account |
| `operation` | Distinguishes UPSERT from DELETE | Only those two operations exist |
| `amount_cents` | Keeps the fictional balance exact | Nonnegative integer; DELETE is zero |
| `occurred_at` | Records time with explicit timezone | Aware ISO-8601 text |

The **source position** is a teaching stand-in. Real MySQL binlog offsets, Kafka offsets or application sequences have much more complex transaction semantics.

## Step 2. Make invalid input fail visibly

The validator rejects negative balances, Boolean money values, malformed IDs, an invalid source version, a DELETE with a nonzero balance and timestamps lacking a timezone.

Run:

~~~bash
cd projects/data-to-decision-platform
python -m unittest discover -v
~~~

A validation check is valuable because its consequences are explicit. Avoid adding rules merely because a form looks impressive; every rejection should protect a known invariant.

## Step 3. Write the business question

We want the **number of active fictional accounts and total active balances for one tenant**. That means:

- Grain: one latest account state per tenant/account.
- Deleted accounts do not contribute to the total.
- Each account contributes exactly once.
- The caller's identity and permitted tenant scope are **out of scope in this standalone demo**, and must be enforced by a real application.
- Integer cents avoid unnecessary binary floating-point rounding.

## Your exercise

Create two additional fictional updates. One should be a correction to an existing account with a higher version; the other should be a deliberately invalid negative value.

Before running the pipeline, predict which batch should commit, which should roll back and what the aggregate will become. Record your predictions. Then run the test.

## What I would ask in a code review

1. Does source position uniquely identify a logical change?
2. Who generates account versions?
3. Could two writers issue conflicting versions?
4. Does the source guarantee global ordering, per-account ordering or neither?
5. Which timestamps are business time versus ingestion time?
6. What is the rule for correcting an error in already-published data?

### Completion test

You can explain every `Event` field, identify a malformed input and state the current-account grain without reading the query.

[Next: Ingestion and transactions →](02_INGESTION_AND_TRANSACTIONS.md)

# Build With Me 02 | Ingest, replay, and fail atomically

[← Source contract](01_SOURCE_AND_CONTRACT.md) · [Volume V](../OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Next: State projection →](03_PROJECTIONS_AND_GRAIN.md)

## A successful batch needs a definition

A common data engineering failure is treating “the process finished” as evidence that every change reached the destination. I look for **durable progress, no unintended duplication, and a recoverable failure state**.

The [Pipeline.apply_batch()](../../projects/data-to-decision-platform/engine.py) example uses SQLite transactions and two tables: a source-event history and the latest-account projection.

## What happens to one event

~~~mermaid
flowchart TD
    E["Input event"] --> V{"Contract valid?"}
    V -->|"No"| RB["Raise error and roll back batch"]
    V -->|"Yes"| ID{"Event ID already seen?"}
    ID -->|"Identical"| DUP["Count duplicate; no state change"]
    ID -->|"Conflicting"| RB
    ID -->|"New"| BR["Insert Bronze event"]
    BR --> VER{"Account version"}
    VER -->|"Older"| ST["Record late event, keep newer projection"]
    VER -->|"Equal conflicting"| RB
    VER -->|"Newer"| UP["Upsert Silver state or tombstone"]
    ST --> COM["Commit entire valid batch"]
    UP --> COM
    DUP --> COM
~~~

The transaction is a toy demonstration using one in-memory SQLite connection. It is **not an end-to-end exactly-once guarantee for an external source**.

## Test 1. Idempotent replay

~~~bash
python cli.py demo
~~~

The CLI inserts eight events, then replays them. On replay, all eight should be recognised as exact duplicates, and the active-account totals should remain unchanged.

**Why this matters:** a consumer restart often causes at-least-once delivery. Correct applications must either tolerate safe replay or explicitly detect duplicates.

## Test 2. Conflicting identity

Change the amount of a previously processed event but keep its `event_id`. The engine should reject it, rather than silently treating it as the old event.

**Why:** if an identifier is reused for a different payload, deduplication has become data corruption.

## Test 3. All-or-nothing batch failure

~~~bash
python cli.py failure
~~~

The CLI deliberately sends a valid update followed by an invalid negative balance. The transaction rolls back the valid update too. The demonstration reports whether the source-event log and state remained unchanged.

**Why:** partial acceptance inside one declared atomic batch is hard to reason about unless explicitly designed.

## Test 4. Source positions

Two different event IDs with the same source position are rejected by a uniqueness constraint. This example assumes unique positions; a real source may identify events using a composite transaction ID, row index and offset.

## What this does not solve

Real capture/processing systems must coordinate reading from a remote source, destination commit and checkpoint acknowledgement. They need crash testing, source retention awareness, backpressure, bounded batches, concurrency rules and operations monitoring.

The [Fixer synthetic CDC review](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241) illustrates why a successful local replay experiment does not replace a real source-adapter test.

## Your exercise

Create an event with a fresh ID but the **same account version** as an existing event. It should fail closed. Then create an older version with a new source position: it should be recorded as historical arrival without overwriting the newer current state.

### Completion test

You can describe the difference between *duplicate event ID*, *same-version conflict*, *stale business update* and *source-position collision*, and demonstrate the expected transaction behaviour.

[← Chapter 01](01_SOURCE_AND_CONTRACT.md) · [Next: State projection →](03_PROJECTIONS_AND_GRAIN.md)

# Build With Me 03 | Model history, current state and business metrics

[← Ingestion](02_INGESTION_AND_TRANSACTIONS.md) · [Volume V](../OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Next: Users and metrics →](04_FROM_METRICS_TO_USERS.md)

## History is not current state

An event log answers **what happened**, and a projection answers **what is true according to the model now**. They are related, but they cannot be treated as interchangeable.

Our simulation uses a deliberately small Bronze/Silver/Gold idea:

- **Bronze:** `bronze_events`, one row per distinct source change.
- **Silver:** `silver_accounts`, one latest logical version per tenant/account. Deletion is represented by a tombstone.
- **Gold:** a query counting active accounts and summing their integer-cent balances by tenant.

These are roles of data, not proof that this is Microsoft Fabric, a Databricks Delta Lake or a managed streaming platform.

## Follow one fictional account

| Event | Business entity | Version | Operation | Silver result |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| evt-01 | alpha/acct-a | 1 | UPSERT 12,000 cents | Active, 12,000 |
| evt-04 | alpha/acct-a | 2 | UPSERT 14,000 cents | Active, 14,000 |
| hypothetical evt-09 | alpha/acct-a | 1 | UPSERT 12,000 cents | Still active, 14,000; historical arrival retained |

When an event arrives out of order, we do not overwrite the more recent state with an older account version.

**Important caveat:** in real source systems, versions may not be strictly monotonic or globally comparable. This educational contract assumes they are.

## Why DELETE becomes a tombstone

An account's disappearance from a snapshot may mean deletion, missing extraction, lost permission or a filter change. The simulation represents DELETE explicitly, preserving evidence in Bronze and marking Silver as deleted.

The Gold query excludes tombstones. It does not claim that a deleted account has been legally erased from all storage. Actual retention and privacy policies would need separate design.

## The grain of the metric

Our business measure is:

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS active_accounts,
       COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0) AS balance_cents
FROM silver_accounts
WHERE tenant = ?
  AND is_deleted = 0;
~~~

Because Silver enforces a primary key on `(tenant, account)`, one account contributes once to the sum. This is not a financial ledger: balances are teaching values without double-entry controls.

## Run and reconcile

~~~bash
python cli.py demo
~~~

The expected synthetic results are 23,000 cents for fictional-alpha and 37,000 cents for fictional-beta, both with two active accounts.

The independent `reconciles()` method creates a separate in-memory database, replays Bronze and compares reconstructed Silver state with the original. If somebody silently corrupts a projection, the comparison should fail.

**Limitation:** replay is only as correct as the event history and model rules. If Bronze itself is incomplete, replaying it perfectly may still reproduce the wrong reality.

## Your exercise

Add a third fictional tenant and two accounts. Verify that the existing tenants' totals remain unchanged. Then corrupt one Silver amount on purpose and prove reconciliation reports false.

### Completion test

You can explain what each layer means, why source identity and business grain are different, and why correct-looking Gold totals are not sufficient without reconciliation to source.

[← Chapter 02](02_INGESTION_AND_TRANSACTIONS.md) · [Next: Users and metrics →](04_FROM_METRICS_TO_USERS.md)

# Build With Me 04 | Take a number from SQL to a useful decision

[← Projections](03_PROJECTIONS_AND_GRAIN.md) · [Volume V](../OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Next: Failure lab →](05_FAILURE_LAB.md)

## A number is only useful inside its meaning

I learned in banking, manufacturing and BI delivery that a dashboard metric is a **contract**. If two people read the same number differently, the software may be technically consistent but operationally misleading.

Our miniature pipeline returns two numbers: active-account count and a sum of fictional balances.

## Define the metric as if it mattered

| Property | Definition in this demo |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Current active-account balance |
| **Audience** | Hypothetical authorised member of one fictional tenant |
| **Grain** | Latest state per tenant/account |
| **Included** | Latest UPSERT versions not marked deleted |
| **Excluded** | DELETE tombstones and stale versions |
| **Currency** | Integer cents as a fictional unit, not a real banking ledger |
| **Time interpretation** | State resulting from applied events, not a guaranteed source-as-of timestamp |
| **Freshness** | The last applied event batch; no external source latency promise |
| **Trust** | Rebuild comparison from Bronze helps detect projection drift |

## Run the local calculation

~~~bash
python cli.py demo
~~~

Find the `alpha_gold` and `beta_gold` JSON objects. Explain why the total for alpha is **23,000** and for beta **37,000**.

Try dividing the total by the number of active accounts. It is mathematically possible, but is “average active-account balance” meaningful for the consumer? That depends on business intent and the distribution, not on how easy the expression is to write.

## The most important security caveat

The lab method `metrics_for(tenant)` takes a caller-provided tenant name and runs parameterised SQL. **That is not authentication or authorisation.** If someone published an HTTP endpoint accepting arbitrary tenant IDs, callers might request other tenants' figures.

In a real product, the server must authenticate the user, resolve their permitted tenant IDs from a trusted identity/relationship store, enforce the requested operation and test cross-tenant denial. The database's read-only role and row-level security can provide additional boundaries.

**Do not put this toy method on the public internet.**

## Your API design exercise

Without implementing a network server, write a design for:

~~~text
GET /api/reports/account-summary

Identity: signed, verified server session
Tenant scope: derived from authorised membership
Permission: reports.read
Response:
  tenant
  active_accounts
  balance_cents
  source_as_of (if the pipeline can truly provide it)
  freshness_status
Denial:
  unauthenticated -> 401
  insufficient permission -> 403
  wrong tenant -> 403/404 with no existence leak
~~~

Now write **negative tests first**: ordinary user, expired session, revoked membership, cross-tenant query, malformed account identifier and unexpected source lag.

## Data visualization exercise

Create a simple bar chart or console table for fictional-alpha and fictional-beta. Choose labels that disclose exactly what is represented. Then deliberately use the wrong label “real-time revenue” and explain why it is false.

**A dashboard tells a story. The best engineer makes sure it tells a true one.**

### Completion test

You can explain the metric to a non-technical person, identify its freshness limitations and design a server-side trust boundary before exposing it to users.

[← Chapter 03](03_PROJECTIONS_AND_GRAIN.md) · [Next: Break the system →](05_FAILURE_LAB.md)

# Build With Me 05 | Break it on purpose and prove the boundaries

[← Metrics to users](04_FROM_METRICS_TO_USERS.md) · [Volume V](../OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Next: Beyond the demo →](06_BEYOND_THE_DEMO.md)

A system that works on the happy path can still be unusable in practice. My method is to **find the failure that changes the user's outcome** and design an experiment that reproduces it.

The [test suite](../../projects/data-to-decision-platform/test_engine.py) contains twenty explicit regression cases. They demonstrate expected behaviour of this fictional Python project, not production security or distributed recovery.

## Failure matrix

| Failure | What might go wrong | What to observe |
|---|---|---|
| Event delivered twice | Duplicate current state or inflated totals | State and Gold totals unchanged |
| Event ID reused with different payload | Silent corruption | Rejection and unchanged committed state |
| Same source position assigned twice | Stream identity ambiguity | Database rejects the collision |
| Same version assigned to conflicting events | Non-deterministic latest state | Fail closed; do not guess the winner |
| Old version arrives late | Historical update overwrites current truth | Store event but preserve later projection |
| Delete arrives | Ghost account remains in aggregate | Tombstone retained, aggregate excludes it |
| Later row is invalid | Earlier row commits from a failed declared batch | Entire batch rolls back |
| Projection manually corrupted | Green process with incorrect state | Independent replay detects mismatch |
| Caller supplies malicious-looking tenant string | Unsafe query interpolation | Input validation and parameterisation |
| Timestamp lacks timezone | Business order becomes ambiguous | Reject at contract boundary |

## How to run the tests

~~~bash
cd projects/data-to-decision-platform
python -m unittest discover -v
python cli.py failure
~~~

The CLI produces `all_or_nothing`, `event_log_unchanged` and `reconciled` flags. Inspect the source rather than trusting flags without understanding how they are computed.

## The test that proves transactions

A good batch includes **a valid update followed by a deliberately invalid update**. If the implementation processes and commits rows one by one, it could leave half the batch accepted.

The demonstration encloses all writes inside one SQLite transaction. A later exception rolls back the earlier uncommitted writes.

**A real distributed source-to-sink system needs more:** the source checkpoint must not advance if the destination commit fails. That boundary doesn't exist in this toy example.

## The test that proves the event identity contract

Replay a previously accepted event ID with the **same payload**: it should do nothing.

Replay the same ID with a **different amount**: it should fail.

If you don't make that distinction, deduplication can silently hide corruption.

## The test that proves business version precedence

Apply account version 2, then a valid but late arrival of version 1 using a new event ID and source position.

The late event should appear in Bronze history but should not replace the newer Silver state. Now try two different events both claiming version 2. The code should reject the conflict rather than picking an arbitrary winner.

## Your deliberate failure exercise

1. Run the complete test suite.
2. Temporarily remove the code path that recognises duplicate event IDs.
3. Run the duplicate test again and observe a failure.
4. Restore the code.
5. Change the Gold filter to include tombstones.
6. Run the aggregate test, observe failure, then restore.
7. Write a journal entry: what invariant did each defect violate?

**Never commit the intentionally broken version as a claimed working solution.**

## A better explanation than “all tests green”

A strong statement is: “At this commit, the synthetic suite verified unique event IDs, replay, conflict rejection, rollback, tombstones, tenant-separated state and projection reconstruction against its own in-memory event history. It did not test external CDC, authentication, durable recovery, distributed consumers or live deployment.”

That is the level of precision I aim for in real engineering releases.

# Build With Me 06 | What it would take to become a real platform

[← Failure lab](05_FAILURE_LAB.md) · [Volume V](../OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [30-Day Expedition](../THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md)

The most useful part of a toy project might be the honesty about what it **cannot** do. A script can prove a local invariant and still be inappropriate for real users.

## The gap from demonstration to operations

| Dimension | In this lab | Production questions |
|---|---|---|
| **Source capture** | In-code fictional events | Which source emits changed rows, offsets, deletes and transactions? |
| **Storage** | SQLite in-memory | Durable backup, retention, migrations, HA and restricted credentials? |
| **Identity** | None | Who authenticated the caller, and who granted the tenant scope? |
| **Checkpoints** | Event position stored in Bronze | How is source acknowledgement atomic with destination commit? |
| **Concurrency** | One process | Multiple readers, concurrent writers, ordering, deadlocks and retries? |
| **Schema evolution** | One fixed dataclass | Versioned source contracts and backwards-compatible migrations? |
| **Quality** | Focused input checks | Completeness, reconciliation, late events, observability and alerts? |
| **Reporting** | One aggregate per tenant | Documented KPIs, as-of semantics, SLO, privacy-safe exports? |
| **Security** | Input validation and parameterised SQL | Auth, authorisation, egress, secrets, RLS, key rotation and negative testing? |
| **Release** | Disposable local test | Staging, load testing, restore, rollback, approval and on-call plan? |

## A staged upgrade plan

### Stage 1. Make the dataset and contracts explicit

Persist synthetic input fixtures in versioned files, add schema documentation and verify that every dataset can be regenerated. Document which identifiers are global versus per account.

### Stage 2. Add durable storage and recovery

Use a disposable local database file or container. Simulate a process restart, database lock and damaged projection. Check whether the event log can rebuild state and whether a restore produces the same answer.

### Stage 3. Connect a real **synthetic** source

Choose a local test MySQL/PostgreSQL service or event queue. Define how to read changes and retain source positions; never connect the learning project to an employer's production database.

### Stage 4. Add real application security

Introduce a trusted identity boundary, tenant memberships, role-specific access and deny-by-default API handlers. Validate cross-tenant denial over real HTTP requests, including ID tampering.

### Stage 5. Serve a consumer

Build one accessible dashboard or reporting API with a visible source-as-of status, structured errors and audit metadata. Do not call it real time until end-to-end freshness is measured.

### Stage 6. Operate and explain

Automate exact-commit tests and build, restore rehearsal, dependency review, logs, metrics, incident playbooks and a rollback procedure. Have another engineer attempt the steps without your machine.

## The true comparison with my professional experience

I have worked on enterprises where source data, access control, reporting metrics, deployment cost and user-facing workflows collide. The public reference projects and independent builds are larger, less tidy and often still being improved.

This synthetic lab is designed to **transfer the habits** without exposing those private operational details. It does not establish that The Fixer or CABO is production-ready.

## What I would look for in a junior engineer's project

I would not demand a complex microservice ecosystem. I would ask:

- Can you explain the authoritative business event?
- Are the keys, joins and time semantics correct?
- Can your code be run from clean setup instructions?
- Have you tested a failed input and an unauthorised action?
- Can you distinguish a tutorial test from a release gate?
- Which decisions would you reconsider at larger scale?

Answer those clearly, and you have something more compelling than a stack-name collection.

## Final assignment

Write a two-page architecture decision record that proposes one safe next step for the project. Include the actual risk, the alternatives, a small disposable experiment, the acceptance tests, the rollback path and a candid limitation.

**My closing principle:** broad engineering ability isn't about writing every component yourself. It's knowing which boundaries need to exist, how to validate them, and when to bring in specialists.

# Chapter 01 | The engineer behind the systems

[Table of contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next: The career →](02_THE_CAREER.md)

## The short version

I'm **Cayelaem Jantjies**, a Johannesburg-based data engineer, analytics engineer and full-stack software developer. My formal foundation is a **BCom in Statistics and Data Science from the University of Pretoria (2023)**. I have over three years of hands-on professional engineering and analytics experience spanning financial services, manufacturing, FMCG, broadcasting, agriculture and social-impact projects.

What differentiates my work is range with continuity. I can follow a problem from an operational source system, through SQL and transformations, into a semantic model, an API, a user interface and the controls required to run it safely.

My role is not simply to report on technology. I build the technology that makes the reporting, workflow or decision possible.

## The version that matters in a project

I often find that the initial request is narrower than the real problem.

> “The report is slow.”

The underlying issue might be an expensive query, ambiguous relationships in the semantic model, repeated API calls or a missing pre-aggregation. Fixing only the loading animation would leave the bottleneck intact.

> “We need real-time dashboards.”

The source may offer only a nullable timestamp with one-second precision. Polling it every minute is not automatically CDC, and a deleted record may never trigger a change. First define the freshness contract, then choose an ingestion design.

> “Can AI mark this answer?”

That question also implies source grounding, rubric consistency, partial credit, appeals, data privacy, educator review, latency and cost. A model call is one component of the workflow.

This is how I think: **follow the failure across boundaries instead of treating every symptom as an isolated ticket**.

## The work I bring to a team

| Practice | What I can contribute | Example evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Data engineering** | SQL modelling, staging, quality checks, source integrations, historical semantics, pipeline debugging | Manufacturing and enterprise BI engagements; [CDC lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/) |
| **Analytics engineering** | Power BI, DAX, Power Query, dimensional modelling, access-aware measures, dashboard performance | Banking, research, agriculture and FMCG; [SQL-plan lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/) |
| **Full-stack delivery** | React, TypeScript, Node.js, API contracts, PostgreSQL/MySQL integration, testing and release processes | [The Fixer](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges), [CABO Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub) |
| **Applied AI** | Structured outputs, evidence-aware evaluations, provider fallback and human-in-the-loop product flows | Learning assessment experiments; [offline evaluation lab](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/) |
| **Security and operations** | Identity, authorisation, MFA workstreams, synthetic integration testing, CI, migrations and rollback | Public security and infrastructure PRs, with release gates still visible |

Not all of these disciplines have the same depth of experience. I distinguish production delivery, hands-on experiments and developing skills instead of assigning myself every fashionable job title on the internet.

## What I believe good engineering looks like

**Correctness before presentation.** The number is only useful when we can explain what was counted, at which grain, with which exclusions and at what time.

**A working system before an impressive diagram.** Architecture earns its value when deployment, failure recovery, access and maintenance are possible.

**Security as a property of workflow.** A beautiful admin screen cannot compensate for weak server-side authorisation or an unsafe database role.

**Care for the user.** The correct solution is one someone can use, understand and trust; unnecessary complexity is a cost to the person on the other side of the application.

**A measurable definition of done.** I look for executable tests, traceable outcomes and clear limitations, not declarations that everything is “production ready.”

## What you will find in this handbook

You will find career history and practical technical explanations together. The former explains where my instincts came from. The latter shows the choices I make when building. Some projects are proprietary, some are public, and some are intentionally small synthetic labs. Each kind of evidence has a different meaning.

**My long-term direction:** evolve from hands-on cross-stack ownership toward solution architecture and technology leadership without losing the technical depth to question a system's assumptions.
